title: Two drops, a hair apart. Same magnet? No. Released 0.1 mm apart: purple and red.
description:
Two drops, a hair apart. Same magnet? Two identical pendulums over a table with three magnets, released from rest one tenth of a millimetre apart. They move as one, then split, and end over different magnets. Seen from above at half speed, twice from the same spot.

Measured (deterministic, no seed):
- string 1 m, drag 0.3 per second, three magnets 6 cm from the centre at 90, 210 and 330 degrees, bob 3 cm above the magnet plane, magnet strength 0.006 m^3/s^2 (pull straight above a magnet 0.68 g), bob 10 mm across, RK4 at 1,200 steps per second
- release point chosen by rule: the nearest 1 mm grid point to (0, 8 cm) whose neighbour 0.1 mm to the right ends at a different magnet; result (-0.05, 7.95) cm
- the gap passes 1 mm at 0.66 s, one ball width (10 mm) at 1.07 s, and 100 mm (a thousand times the release gap) at 3.29 s
- the white ball settles over the purple magnet at 7.85 s, the gold ball over the red magnet at 7.96 s (within 5 mm, under 5 mm/s)
- basin map, 200 x 200 release points 1 mm apart over a 20 cm square: 41.7 percent of points end at a different magnet from their neighbour 1 mm to the right; 26.9 percent differ from a neighbour 0.1 mm to the right
- check at 2,400 steps per second: same split time, same magnets; released 1 mm apart: split at 0.66 s, purple and blue; 10 mm apart: split at 0.22 s, purple and blue

Why: three magnets make the pull on the ball change direction sharply between them, so every pass near a magnet bends two nearly identical swings a little differently and the difference compounds. The equations have no randomness; the outcome is decided by the start to a fraction of a hair (a chaotic magnetic pendulum).

The numbers in the narration are the printed outputs of this exact run.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
